t: Audio Transcription Tool: a plain-language overview
title: Audio Transcription Tool: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Audio Transcription Tool does and why archives need it. An audio transcription tool listens to a recording and writes down the words it hears. It first finds the parts that actually contain speech, then converts those parts into text, one chunk at a time. The result is a written transcript with timestamps, so you can jump straight to the moment a word was spoken.
demo:
# Audio Transcription Tool - runnable demo (JAH-ATK154-000001)
RANK = 1
SIG = False
FRAMES = [0.05, 0.08, 0.5, 0.6, 0.55, 0.1, 0.06, 0.48, 0.52, 0.07]  # short-time energy per 20ms frame
WORDS = ["the","archive","holds","many","voices","from","distant","years","today","we","listen"]
def vad(frames, thresh=0.35):
    segs, start = [], None
    for i, e in enumerate(frames):
        if e >= thresh and start is None: start = i
        elif e < thresh and start is not None:
            segs.append((start, i-1)); start = None
    if start is not None: segs.append((start, len(frames)-1))
    return [s for s in segs if s[1]-s[0] >= 1]
segs = vad(FRAMES)
print("speech segments (frames):", segs)
transcript = []
for k, (a, b) in enumerate(segs):
    chunk_words = WORDS[k*2:(k+1)*2] or WORDS[:1]
    t0, t1 = a*0.02, (b+1)*0.02
    transcript.append((t0, t1, " ".join(chunk_words)))
for t0, t1, w in transcript:
    print("[%.2fs-%.2fs] %s" % (t0, t1, w))
if RANK >= 3:
    avg_e = sum(FRAMES)/len(FRAMES)
    print("mean frame energy: %.3f | segments kept: %d/%d frames speech" % (avg_e, sum(b-a+1 for a,b in segs), len(FRAMES)))
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-AUD-" + "JAH-ATK154-000001")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK154-000001", "OK")

t: How the Audio Transcription Tool works

t: How the Audio Transcription Tool works: the deep tour
title: How the Audio Transcription Tool works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Audio Transcription Tool does and why archives need it. Real transcription pipelines start with voice activity detection (VAD), which uses short-time energy and zero-crossing rate to cut long recordings into speech segments and skip silence. Each segment becomes acoustic features — historically MFCCs, in modern systems log-mel spectrograms — fed to a neural acoustic model trained with CTC or attention-based sequence loss, the approach behind systems like Whisper and wav2vec 2.0. A language model rescores hypotheses, and forced alignment maps each word back to its audio timestamps. Quality is measured by word error rate against human transcripts. Production systems add noise suppression, automatic language identification, and punctuation restoration, and they stream results with partial hypotheses for live use. Speaker diarization (tool 155, skipped here as covered elsewhere) can be layered on to label who spoke when. Limits are heavy accents, overlapping speech, and domain jargon — all raise word error rates — so professional archives keep a human review pass and record confidence scores per word rather than presenting machine text as verbatim truth.

t: Accuracy, evaluation, and limits of the Audio Transcription Tool
title: Accuracy, evaluation, and limits of the Audio Transcription Tool
description: Evaluation: how the Audio Transcription Tool is tested, where it is accurate, and where it reaches its limits. Real transcription pipelines start with voice activity detection (VAD), which uses short-time energy and zero-crossing rate to cut long recordings into speech segments and skip silence. Each segment becomes acoustic features — historically MFCCs, in modern systems log-mel spectrograms — fed to a neural acoustic model trained with CTC or attention-based sequence loss, the approach behind systems like Whisper and wav2vec 2.0. A language model rescores hypotheses, and forced alignment maps each word back to its audio timestamps. Quality is measured by word error rate against human transcripts. Production systems add noise suppression, automatic language identification, and punctuation restoration, and they stream results with partial hypotheses for live use. Speaker diarization (tool 155, skipped here as covered elsewhere) can be layered on to label who spoke when. Limits are heavy accents, overlapping speech, and domain jargon — all raise word error rates — so professional archives keep a human review pass and record confidence scores per word rather than presenting machine text as verbatim truth.
demo:
# Audio Transcription Tool - runnable demo (JAH-ATK154-000012)
RANK = 3
SIG = False
FRAMES = [0.04, 0.45, 0.5, 0.47, 0.05, 0.06, 0.52, 0.49, 0.55, 0.03]  # short-time energy per 20ms frame
WORDS = ["the","archive","holds","many","voices","from","distant","years","today","we","listen"]
def vad(frames, thresh=0.35):
    segs, start = [], None
    for i, e in enumerate(frames):
        if e >= thresh and start is None: start = i
        elif e < thresh and start is not None:
            segs.append((start, i-1)); start = None
    if start is not None: segs.append((start, len(frames)-1))
    return [s for s in segs if s[1]-s[0] >= 1]
segs = vad(FRAMES)
print("speech segments (frames):", segs)
transcript = []
for k, (a, b) in enumerate(segs):
    chunk_words = WORDS[k*2:(k+1)*2] or WORDS[:1]
    t0, t1 = a*0.02, (b+1)*0.02
    transcript.append((t0, t1, " ".join(chunk_words)))
for t0, t1, w in transcript:
    print("[%.2fs-%.2fs] %s" % (t0, t1, w))
if RANK >= 3:
    avg_e = sum(FRAMES)/len(FRAMES)
    print("mean frame energy: %.3f | segments kept: %d/%d frames speech" % (avg_e, sum(b-a+1 for a,b in segs), len(FRAMES)))
